"VITAMINS - EVERY SINGLE DAY
The floor you never drop below. Not a workout - the thing that makes the workout possible.
No standards, no scoring, no skipping. If you are in the gym, this happened.
About 20 minutes. Same order every day so you never think about it.

HANDLING - stationary, both hands, eyes up the whole time
1 high 1 low
rapid switch
low around the leg
under the low arm
hi ho
figure 8

HANDLING - on the move
skips through and backwards
lowmans
misdirection through and behind

TOUCH AT THE RIM
Regular mikans
Wide 1 foot mikans
Spin mikans high and low
Spin mikans 1 side
Floaters around the arc

VITAMINS PROPER - your daily dose of counters
Killer cross to burnsey
In and out to spin layup
Reverse through to euro

FORM
5 one-hand form shots, each hand

JUMP TOUCH - Pickens series
5 Pickens 3 jumps
5 Pickens 1 leg
5 Pickens side jump
5 Pickens lateral bound
5 Pickens jump backs
5 Pickens three through pickups

CLOSE
10 one leg chair
10 chair high arcs
10 threes, then free throws to leave

WHAT CHANGED FROM YOUR OLD WARMUP
Nothing was removed. It was one long list and is now grouped by what each part is for, so a day
you are short on time you cut a GROUP, not a random line. If you have to cut, cut Jump Touch -
it is the one thing your lift already covers."

Read this once. It turns the one number you already produce every day into a real one.

WHEN
End of the afternoon block, both halves, back to back. Shooting them tired is the better rep and
it means you log the whole day in one moment instead of carrying a number around since morning.

THE 50 THREES - 5 racks of 10, always these spots, always this order
1. Right corner - 10
2. Right wing - 10
3. Top of the key - 10
4. Left wing - 10
5. Left corner - 10
Type each rack the second it ends. Five small numbers beat one number at the end.
WHY THIS MATTERS: without fixed spots, 34/50 from the corners and 34/50 from the top look identical
in your log and they are not the same day. Undefined spots are why the number never meant anything.

THE 50 FREE THROWS - 5 sets of 10
Sets of 10 only so you never have to hold a count past ten.

LOG IT
One row in the Log table: date, threes out of 50, free throws out of 50.
78 rows exist and at six days a week they run out in mid-November. Add more before the season.

WHAT A GOOD DAY IS
You do not know yet, and that is the point. Shoot it for ten days, then your line gets set from
your own numbers rather than from a guess. Until then the only job is putting a row in the table."},{"title":"Log","type":"table","columns":["Date","Threes/50","Free Throws/50"],"rows":[["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""],["","",""]]}]},"4":{"sel":0,"pages":[{"title":"Conditioning","body":"AEROBIC

Attach this to the END of your bag work, twice a week. It is a finisher, not a session.
Games are played tired. Every other skill block in your program is done fresh.
Pick one and rotate. About 10 minutes.

1. MAKE OR REPEAT
Pick a bag package. You do not leave a drill until you hit its written standard.
Miss the standard and the whole drill runs again. No partial credit.

2. SHOOTING ON EMPTY
Sprint the floor twice, then shoot 5 from the wing. Five rounds.
Track makes out of 25. This is the honest number, not your fresh one.

3. FREE THROWS TIRED
Every time you finish a hard block anywhere in your day, shoot 2 free throws before you sit down.
Log makes out of the day's total attempts.

4. BEAT THE CLOCK
Shot clock on your phone. 30 seconds to get a specific shot off a specific action.
10 rounds. Do not get the shot off and it counts as a miss.

5. ONE MINUTE SPOTS
60 seconds at one spot, as many makes as you can. Rest 60. Five spots.
Log total makes and compare month to month.

LOG IT - here, overwrite it each time
LAST RUN: drill ___   number ___   date ___
The number here will always be worse than your fresh number. That is the point.
When the gap between tired and fresh shrinks, you are actually getting somewhere."}]},"5":{"sel":0,"pages":[{"title":"Partner Menu","body":"PARTNER MENU
Grab one of these when somebody is in the gym with you. 20 minutes, zero planning.
This REPLACES the passing block that day. Live reads beat wall reps every time.
Pick by what you have not done recently, not by what you feel like doing.

1. LIVE PASSING READS - 20 min
He plays help off your drive. He commits or he does not and you read it.
Drive and read 6x ea side, then ball screen with him as the coverage 10x ea side.
The only rule: he never tells you what he is doing beforehand.

2. ONE ON ONE, FULL - 20 min
Live, both ends. First to 7, win by 2. Write the score down.
Pick what you are hunting before you start, same as a practice intention.

3. CLOSEOUT AND CONTAIN, LIVE - 20 min
He starts with the ball on the wing, you start under the rim. You close, he attacks.
6 reps then switch. You win the rep if he never gets a straight-line drive.

4. SCREEN NAVIGATION, LIVE - 20 min
He comes off a screen you have to get through. Over, under, or top lock - call it before the rep.
8 reps ea side then switch.

5. CONTESTED SHOOTING - 20 min
He closes out for real, you shoot for real. 20 off the catch, 20 off the dribble.
Track makes. Compare it to your 50/50 number - the gap is what pressure costs you.

6. REBOUNDING AND BOX OUT - 20 min
Live box out off a shot. First to 10 rebounds.
The most under-trained thing a guard can do with a partner.

LOG IT - here, overwrite it each time
LAST RUN: drill ___   score ___   date ___
If you have not run one of these in three weeks, that is the one you do next."},{"title":"Practice Intentions","body":"PRACTICE INTENTIONS
Live reps without a target are just cardio. Pick ONE before every practice and every run.
One. Not three. You cannot hunt three things at once and you will end up hunting none.
Write it on the line below before you go, and score yourself out of 10 after.
TODAY: ___                                 AFTER: ___ /10
LAST PRACTICE: ___                         ___ /10

DEFENSE
I do not get beat baseline once.
I get over every ball screen. No going under unless I call it first.
I am in a stance before he catches, not after.
I finish possessions - I box out every single time a shot goes up.
I talk on every screen. Every one.

PASSING AND DECISIONS
I hit the roller at least three times.
I make the extra pass every time I am two feet from a good shot and someone has a better one.
Zero live-dribble turnovers.
I look weak side before I pick up my dribble.
I throw at least one skip pass.

SCORING
I get to a left-hand finish twice.
No contested twos.
I shoot every open catch-and-shoot without hesitating.
I get downhill off the first side action instead of the third.

MOVEMENT AND COMPETE
I sprint the floor both ways every possession of one full drill.
My hips stay low through every screen I navigate.
I stop on one step, not three.

HOW TO USE IT
Rotate through them. Do not repeat one until you have scored yourself 8 or better on it twice.
A 4 out of 10 is more useful than a 9 - it tells you what to hunt next time.
The point is not the score. The point is that you walked in looking for something."},{"title":"PRACTICE - TRANSITION AND READS","body":"PRACTICE - TRANSITION AND READS

Read this before practice. Pick two. Not five, two. Score yourself out of 10 after, on the line below.
PICKED: ___ and ___          AFTER: ___ /10 and ___ /10

This page exists because these are the things that cannot be repped alone. Reps Transition grooves the movement. This is where the deciding gets trained, and Tuesday is the only day it can happen.

TRANSITION OFFENSE
First look is up the floor on every rebound and every make, before the ball goes down. Count the possessions I looked first.
Push past the free throw line before I decide anything. No decision made above the arc.
Name the advantage to myself every break. Numbers, mismatch, or none. If none, pull it out on the first beat instead of driving into a set defense.
Every break ends one of three ways. I finish it, I hit the man ahead, or I pull it out clean. No dead dribble in the middle third.
When I am not the ball, I run wide to the corner every time. No drifting to the wing early.
As the trail man I am ready before the catch, and I shoot it in one motion if it is there.

TRANSITION DEFENSE
Paint first, man second. Get to the paint, then find who I have.
I take the most dangerous man, not my man, until we are matched up.
I talk on every get back. Call the ball, call who I have, out loud, every possession.
My first step after my own shot is back. Count the possessions I lost that step.

READING A CLOSEOUT
Three options on the catch and I decide on the catch, not before it. Shoot it. Attack the high shoulder. One more, and relocate.

BALL SCREEN, THE LATE READ
I do not decide before I leave. I read the coverage after the first dribble, not at the point of the screen. If I know the answer before I come off it, that was a bag rep, not a live one.
Hedge and blitz are the two coverages I have never repped anywhere. Those are the ones to go looking for at practice."},{"title":"GROUP WORKOUT IDEAS - parked","body":"GROUP WORKOUT IDEAS - PARKED
Everything that needs a body. Nothing here is scheduled. We look at this after the solo system
is finished.

WHY THIS PAGE EXISTS
Contact and physicality came out of every solo page on purpose. A wall does not move, does not
recover, and does not push back - training contact against one teaches you to lean, not to move
somebody. All of it lives here until there is a person on the other side of it.

CONTACT - pulled out of the solo pages
Finish through a bump. Take the hit on the way up and let it change nothing about the finish.
Attack into contact, absorb it, counter off it into the finish. The counter is the point.
Navigate a screen with a real body in it - get skinny, take the hit, keep the line.
Hold your line while somebody rides your hip. Keep the path and keep the height.
Play through a bump on the catch before you shoot.
Post-up and seal work - anything where you move a body off a spot.

DEFENSE THAT NEEDS A PERSON
Deny work. You said you are open to this in a group.
Live one on one, full court and half court. The real version of everything on the Defense page.
Guarding a real screen where the screener actually screens.
Help and recover with a second offensive player who punishes a late closeout.
Post defense and guarding up a size.

PASSING AND READS THAT NEED A PERSON
Live-dribble passing where the help defender actually commits, so the read is real.
Two on one and three on two - the decision, not the delivery.
Off-ball cutting and screening timing, where arriving early or late actually costs something.

WHAT A PARTNER IS WORTH MOST FOR
Not more reps. Reps you can get alone. A partner is worth the things that cannot be faked:
a defender who reacts, contact that moves you, and a passer whose timing is not your own.
Spend partner time on those and nothing else."}]},"6":{"sel":1,"pages":[{"title":"Movement - Drive Position","body":"MOVEMENT - DRIVE POSITION
Every rep at stride height. Hips come up, the rep is over.

Low Stride Walk - 1x10, hold the bottom 2s
Low Stride Walk, no hold - 2x10
Low Drive Steps, half speed - 3x ea, 3 steps
Low Drive Steps, full speed - 4x ea, 3 steps
Low Drive to Low Stop - 4x ea, stop in 2 steps, hold 2s
Low Drive, Stop, Go back the other way - 3x ea
Low Drive to Cut - 3x ea, 45 degrees off the outside foot at the cone
Single-Leg Low Landing - 2x3 ea, from an angle, stick 2s

BUILD IT
Same ladder every day. The build is speed at the same height, then a stop, then a cut, then a call.
Stops - 2 steps until it is silent, then 1 step.
Cuts - sharper angle, later cut, then on a Split Second call (Left / Right).
Landings - further out, steeper angle.

FIRST SESSION OF THE MONTH
5-10-5 ___ s / ___ s
Steps to stop from a full-court sprint ___"},{"title":"Defense","body":"DEFENSE
25-30 min, after the bag. Every rep at stance height. Hips come up, the rep is over.
Nothing here is scored on makes. Levels per drill. 2-3 drills a session.

1. LOW AND FAST                                               NOW: L___
Cover the lane low. Slide 3, open the hip and sprint 3, re-plant, slide 3. Stance height the whole way.
  L1  Game speed
  L2  Full speed, tape a mark at stance height, never above it
  L3  Slide 3, sprint 5, slide 3
  L4  Baseline to half court, low the whole way
  L5  Race the clock, Split Second Chase mode, beat your best time
  L6  Tired

2. STICK IT LOW                                               NOW: L___
Full speed into a one-leg stop, stuck in stance, 2 seconds, no wobble. Your own momentum is the contact.
  L1  Slide 3, stop on the outside foot
  L2  Sprint 3, stop on one foot in stance
  L3  Bound sideways into the one-leg stance, stick it
  L4  Land off balance on purpose, recover into stance, hold
  L5  Stick it, then push straight into the opposite direction
  L6  Which foot called late (Split Second Left / Right)
  L7  Tired

3. CLOSE AND CUT                                              NOW: L___
Full sprint at the cone, the shooter. Brake, cut 45 degrees to the spot, beat the drive there.
  L1  From 10 ft, stop in 2, cut to the spot
  L2  From the arc
  L3  Full sprint from half court
  L4  Cut called late as you arrive (Split Second Left / Right)
  L5  Spot further out, sharper cut
  L6  Stop in 1
  L7  Tired

4. PRESS TURN                                                 NOW: L___
Full court, low. Sprint 4 at an angle, cut, sprint 4 the other way. Turn the dribbler every cut.
  L1  Half court, 3 cuts, game speed
  L2  Full court, 5 cuts
  L3  Full speed, every cut off the outside foot
  L4  Cuts called late (Split Second Left / Right)
  L5  He beats you, cut into a re-plant and backpedal, then sprint again

Closeout D was cut - Recover and Slide covers it. The braking half is Closeout Stop on the Defense page."},{"title":"RECORDING - Does It Sell","body":"RECORDING - DOES IT SELL

10 min a night, off court. Three layers, one number each.
Not in season, so no film of you. Everything below runs on other people's film until there is.

1. KNOWLEDGE - what you know                                  NOW: ___ / 109 taught
The syllabus is the next page. Learn a topic in this order: watch it, draw it, then teach it out loud in 60 seconds with no notes.
Never re-read. Write it from memory or it does not count.
  L1  Name it
  L2  Draw it, every spot
  L3  Teach it out loud, 60s, no notes
  L4  Name the counter and the read that triggers it
  L5  Spot it on film at the entry pass
A topic is TAUGHT at L3. Date it on the syllabus.

2. RECOGNITION - how early you see it
NOW: ball screen L___   closeout L___   help L___   transition L___
Any game on film. Freeze it, call it out loud, play it, score it. 20 clips in 10 min, one situation a night.
The ladder is how early the freeze is. Move up at 8 of 10.
  L1  Frozen at contact - screen set, closeout arrived, break already on
  L2  Frozen as it starts - screener arriving, defender leaving his spot, rebound secured
  L3  Frozen before it starts - screener leaving his man, pass in the air
  L4  Frozen at the entry - nothing has happened yet, call what is coming
Ball screen: the coverage. Closeout: short or long, which hip is open. Help: who is low man, who tags. Transition: numbers, who has it.

3. DECISION - how fast you act on it                          NOW: L___
Same clips, second call. After the coverage, call the play before the clip resumes: shoot, pocket, reject, snake, swing, drive it, take the numbers.
One second to say it or the rep is a miss.
  L1  Coverage, then decision, no clock
  L2  Decision inside one second
  L3  Both calls inside one second
  L4  Both calls from the L3 freeze
  L5  Both calls from the L4 freeze
The if-then for every read is on the syllabus, written from memory before you watch. That is why it is fast in a game.
On the court this layer is Split Second and Practice Intentions.

SOURCES
Film: full games, any level. Coaching breakdown channels for the actions. One guard built like you, one game a week, steal one thing.
Read: DeVenzio, Stuff Good Players Should Know. Oliver, Basketball on Paper. Taylor, Thinking Basketball.

IN SEASON, ADD
Own film after every game: live-dribble turnovers ___   better pass passed up ___   beaten off the dribble ___
A PLAYBOOK page: every team action, your job, the counter, the if-then. Layer 1 runs on that first."},{"title":"IQ - THE SYLLABUS","body":"IQ - THE SYLLABUS

The system for your goal, in your words: unwavering confidence and total control over your nervous system.
Built 9/23 from Nick's material (Polaris, the Vortex, his SOPs and videos) and the performance research. It replaces NERVOUS SYSTEM - Hot and Cold.

WHAT THE GOAL MEANS ONCE IT IS TRAINED
Unwavering - doubt can show up. It does not get a vote. You are back within one breath.
Total control - you move your state up or down on command, in seconds, with your heart rate up and people watching.
Nick's own position: fear never fully leaves. The goal is courage, not fearlessness.

WHERE YOU START
Your Polaris intake: 7-8 out of 10 most games, 4-5 under more pressure. The trigger: fear of judgment.
At 10 out of 10 you tune out the crowd, feel twitchy, stop thinking about single actions and shoot effortlessly.
This whole system has one job: close that gap.

THE LOGIC
Confidence is specific to the situation. In a big moment your brain goes looking for blue: proof you have done this before.
It finds blue where you made it. Most of yours was made in normal conditions, so under pressure it comes up short and doubt fills the space.
This system makes blue under pressure, on purpose.
"We fall to the level of our training, not to the level of our beliefs." - Nick

CONFIDENCE - program it three ways
TELL IT - I am lines, your ethos, belief alarms, the vision board. -> DAILY BASE
SHOW IT - the High Pressure Visualization: mistake, reset, execute. -> HIGH PRESSURE VISUALIZATION
PROVE IT - stakes on your own reps, and every win goes on the list. -> PRESSURE, BLUE LIST
Proof is what makes the other two believable. "I am a killer" lands when you have the receipts.

CONTROL - shift gears on command, in three places
AT REST - your morning and night routine, each piece with a job. -> DAILY BASE
UNDER LOAD - the same tools with your heart rate up and something on the line. -> PRESSURE
LIVE - the door, free throws, the reset, gone cold, check-in, sub-out. -> GAME DAY
You already have AT REST. UNDER LOAD is the missing level, and it is the one that makes LIVE work.

JUDGMENT - your trigger, trained on purpose
Being watched is the main stake on every pressure rep. One small being-seen rep a day outside the gym. -> PRESSURE
Nick: the ego is a scared kid chasing acceptance. Give it the acceptance yourself, first. Then go play.

START ORDER - one layer at a time. A plan you run beats a perfect plan you drop.
WEEK 1
- DAILY BASE: same routine, each piece with its job. No new time.
- BLUE LIST: your first 10 rows, from your whole career, in one sitting.
- PRESSURE TEST: run it once. That is your baseline.
- SLEEP: same wake time every day. Phone down 30 minutes before bed.
- Team sessions and pickup: the door and the reset off GAME DAY.
WEEK 2
- Stakes on the last set of every shooting workout. The free-throw routine on every free throw.
- HIGH PRESSURE VISUALIZATION, 3 mornings a week.
- Rewrite the vision board for this season, with your I am lines and ethos. It is still last season's: NEPSAC, Villanova, 30 a game.
WEEK 3
- Being-seen list written. One rep a day.
- Belief alarms, 3 a day.
OFFICIAL PRACTICE
- All of GAME DAY, every practice. Practice is the pressure lab now: a real coach, real teammates, real judgment.
FITBIT
- The control test starts the week it lands. HRV needs about two weeks before its trend means anything.
EVERY 4 WEEKS
- Read the SCOREBOARD. Keep what moves the numbers. Change or cut what does not.

SCOREBOARD - no mood scores. Only what you do and what your body does.
PRESSURE GAP - free throws normal vs with stakes. The number that matters most. Goal: no gap, then better when it counts.
CONTROL - how many extra beats the DOWN breath drops you after a sprint.
BOLT - Nick's breath number, once a week.
HRV - read it in the Fitbit app. Background only. It reads your system, it never grades a day.

RULES
Blue only before and during games. The red gets one look, on film, then it is closed.
Long holds (Vortex, Wim Hof) lying down or sitting on the floor or bed. Never standing, walking, on a bench, in water or driving.
End every hold at the first real urge. Never push past it. Nick has passed out doing exactly that.
Left out on purpose: holds past the urge, sungazing, the fasting and detox protocols, and any supplement that is not NSF Certified for Sport. A contaminated one costs you your eligibility.

WHEN IT IS BIGGER THAN A PAGE
If the panic from that first practice comes back, take it to someone. CWRU counselling is free, and a sports psych is standard equipment at the level you are chasing. It is a tool, same as a lift."},{"title":"DAILY BASE","body":"DAILY BASE - at rest
What you already do, with a job for each piece. The only new time is the visualization mornings.
Nick's rule for the first and last stretch of the day: program yourself or be programmed. No phone until the morning base is done. Phone down 30 minutes before bed.

MORNING - your lines, your order

MEDITATE - job: return reps.
Every time your mind wanders and you catch it, run the 6 R's: recognize, release, relax, re-smile, rebreathe, return.
Wandering is not failure. Catching it and coming back IS the rep, and it is the same rep as catching doubt mid-game.

VORTEX - job: shift gears, and stay calm while your body sounds the alarm.
The exhale holds are Nick's command training: staying relaxed and in charge while your body starts to sound the alarm. That is what pressure feels like in your body.
Lying down, or sitting on the floor or bed. End each hold at the first real urge.

HIGH PRESSURE VISUALIZATION - 3 mornings a week, right after Vortex. 10 minutes. Its own page.

JOURNAL THE DAY OUT - three lines, then out loud.
TODAY I HUNT - one thing. Practice days: off Practice Intentions.
BEING SEEN - today's rep, off your list on PRESSURE.
I AM - three lines off your vision board, out loud, chest up. Then your ethos, once.

ONCE A WEEK - BOLT, before Vortex (Nick's Bolt Score SOP)
Sit. Breathe out normally through your nose. Pinch your nose and time it until the first definite urge to breathe. Not a max hold.
Same time, same position every week. The number goes on the SCOREBOARD.

DURING THE DAY - belief alarms
Nick's RAS alarms. 3 a day, times are yours. Name each alarm with its question.
1. What am I thinking right now? Name the feeling in one word - naming it takes the charge out. Then the 6 R's.
2. Why am I the hardest guard in the gym to stop? Answer it with real reasons. Swap in your own question.
3. What did I do today that proves it? If the answer is nothing yet, go make one.

NIGHT - your journal line, in this order. 5 minutes.
RED - one line. A moment today you played small, to look good or to not look bad, and what you do instead next time. Then close it. Red never goes to bed with you. Game nights: skip it, the red goes to film.
BLUE - three wins. At least one from a moment you were nervous or watched. The best one goes on the BLUE LIST.
NEXT - the energy you bring into tomorrow. Your line already asks this.

SLOW BREATHE - job: shift down for sleep.
4-7-8, or 4 in and 6 out, lying down. Longer out than in is the only rule.

SLEEP - one of the biggest levers on how reactive your nervous system is.
One sleepless night raised anxiety up to 30% in a Berkeley study. Stanford basketball players who slept more shot about 9 percentage points better from the line and from three.
Same wake time every day, weekends within an hour. 8+ hours in bed.
The Fitbit will show you what you actually get. Believe it over your guess.

YOUR LINES - write them here, keep them here
ETHOS - your shield. One line in your own name, said the second doubt shows up. Talking to yourself by name measurably cuts anxiety when people are judging you.
I'm Alex Hickey, and ___
I AM - three for this season: ___ / ___ / ___
WORD OF THE SEASON (last year: ASSERTIVENESS): ___"},{"title":"PRESSURE","body":"PRESSURE - under load
The missing level. Skills you trained calm do not show up on their own when your heart is pounding and people are watching. They have to be trained there.
In a Dutch study, experienced basketball players who practiced free throws under pressure held their percentage in a pressure test. The ones who practiced normally dropped.
Nick: trigger yourself so often that nothing can shake you.

THE ONE RULE - it only counts if you feel it
Stakes you do not feel are just reps. If your heart rate does not jump, raise them. If you fall apart, drop a notch.
The sweet spot: nervous, and still executing.

THE STAKES - three kinds. One is mild, two is real, three is a game.
CONSEQUENCE - miss and you run, restart the set, or you do not leave until the number is hit. Compete + Fatigue already has these.
FATIGUE - shoot with your heart rate up, right after sprints or at the end of conditioning. Compete + Fatigue has these too.
JUDGMENT - your trigger, so it is the main one. Someone watching and counting. Your number called out loud first. Filmed, and the film goes to someone. A partner talking while you shoot.
Raise it as the gap closes. A live watcher beats a camera. A teammate beats a stranger. A coach beats a teammate.

EVERY SHOOTING WORKOUT - the last set carries stakes
At least one kind. Judgment whenever anyone is around to use.
The free-throw routine on every free throw, and the reset after every miss. Both are on GAME DAY.
Heart pounding at the line: one DOWN breath first. That is control under load.
End on a make. Nick: your nervous system remembers the last rep. If the last one misses, go again.

THE PRESSURE TEST - once a week, same test every time so the numbers compare. About 15 minutes.
ROUND A, NORMAL - 10 pairs of free throws. One down-and-back sprint before each pair. Nothing on the line.
Rest 3 minutes.
ROUND B, STAKES - 10 pairs, the same sprint before each. Phone filming the whole round. Call your number out loud before you start. Anyone in the gym watches and counts. Every miss is 10 push-ups after the round.
LOG IT on the SCOREBOARD like a score, makes out of 20: A-B, e.g. 17-14. GAP = A minus B.
Judge the gap over 4 weeks, not one. Twenty shots is a small sample.
Your first test is your baseline. Run it before anything else on this page.

BEING SEEN - daily, outside the gym
Nick: your nervous system's capacity to be seen grows with exposure, in small doses, every day.
Write your list: 10 things that make you feel watched or judged, easiest to hardest. Do one a day, picked in your morning journal. Start near the middle. When one stops spiking you, move up.
Starters - rewrite them into your own:
- Speak first in a class discussion.
- Be the loudest voice in a drill. Call every screen.
- Shoot alone on the main court when the gym is full.
- Ask the coach for the hardest feedback they have on you. Just say thanks.
- Post a workout clip.
- Say out loud the goal you usually keep to yourself.
MY LIST
1. ___
2. ___
3. ___
4. ___
5. ___
6. ___
7. ___
8. ___
9. ___
10. ___
NOW ON: ___

CONTROL UNDER LOAD
Rest intervals are control reps. In conditioning, every rest is DOWN breaths: two inhales through the nose, one long slow exhale.
CONTROL TEST - weekly, once the Fitbit lands. One session:
1. Sprint 3 down-and-backs. Note your heart rate. Stand still 60 seconds, breathing normally. Note it again.
2. Rest until you are back near where you started.
3. Same sprint. This time 60 seconds of DOWN breaths. Note it again.
CONTROL = how many more beats you dropped with the DOWN breath. It goes in the Ctrl column. Swap which one goes first each week.
Fitness makes both drops bigger. Only the difference is control."},{"title":"HIGH PRESSURE VISUALIZATION","body":"HIGH PRESSURE VISUALIZATION - show it
Nick's pressure protocol, rebuilt around your game. 3 mornings a week, right after Vortex. 10 minutes.
It rehearses the part that actually goes wrong: the mistake, and what you do next.
Picturing only the win feels great and does less, because your brain half-books it as done. The rep is the recovery.

EVERY SCENE, FIVE STEPS
1. BUILD IT - first person, through your own eyes, in real time. The gym, the noise, the score, the clock, who is watching. Add detail until your body reacts. Nick wants a disgusting amount of detail.
2. THE MISTAKE - let it happen. The miss, the turnover, the look from the bench. Feel it for real: the heat, the tight chest, the voice. Do not skip this. This is the rep.
3. THE RESET - your real reset at real speed. The cue, one DOWN breath, the 6 R's in one breath, your ethos, eyes to the next job. Exactly what you will do in the game.
4. THE NEXT PLAY - full speed. You attack. Feel it leave your hand. See it go in. Feel what it is like to be the guy who bounced back.
5. LOCK IT - one line of gratitude. Then: whatever this game gives me, I can handle it.

THE SCENES - rotate them. Rewrite each one in your own detail.
1. THE WALK-IN - a practice like your first one here. New coach watching, big roster, nothing proven. First rep, you fumble the pass. Reset. Next rep you attack the rim.
2. THE LINE - two free throws, down one, four seconds left, their student section behind the basket. The first one rims out. Reset. Routine. The second is pure, and in overtime you want the ball.
3. THE TURNOVER - first possession after you check in. You throw it away and the coach is up off the bench. Reset. Sprint back, get the stop, and next time down you attack the closeout.
4. THE AUDITION - a D1 coach in the stands. You miss your first three. Reset. Next open catch, no hesitation. It goes.
5. YOUR WORST - write the one that scares you most. That is the one that pays the most.
___

ONCE A WEEK - THE VISION (Nick's Peak Performance session, with one fix)
See the finished season. The offer, the moment, who is there. Feel it.
Then see the obstacle inside you that could stop it: the voice, the hesitation.
Then the plan: when that shows up, I ___.
Never end on the dream alone. In the research, dream plus obstacle plus plan beats dreaming alone.

ONCE A WEEK - IN THE GYM
Run THE LINE standing at the real line, ball in hand, eyes open, real time. The closer the imagery is to the real thing, the more it carries over."},{"title":"GAME DAY","body":"GAME DAY - live
Every practice and every game. This is where the other pages cash in.
Built from NERVOUS SYSTEM - Hot and Cold, the page it replaces, plus your Polaris routines and Nick's tools.

THE LOOP - why the first practice went the way it went
Nerves put the body in threat mode. Under threat it protects instead of performing. That is the weak feeling.
With nothing to hunt, "don't mess up" fills the slot. Avoidance makes you slow, slow makes mistakes, and each one confirms the threat.
A loop breaks at any link. Everything below cuts one.

THE TWO GEARS
DOWN - two inhales through the nose, a full one then a short top-up, then one long slow exhale out the mouth. The quickest tool you have for bringing yourself down. For too hot.
UP - short sharp inhales through the nose, quick exhales, and MOVE. Sprint, jump, slap the floor. For flat or cold.
Nerves and excitement are the same body. Only the label differs. Say "I'm excited." Never "calm down."

THE NIGHT BEFORE
The visualization scene closest to tomorrow. Read the BLUE LIST. Slow Breathe. Sleep.

BEFORE - 2 minutes, seated, in the locker room
1. Nick's quick Vortex: 3 seconds in, 3 out. 2 in, 2 out. 1 in, 1 out. Then a short, easy hold - a few seconds, nowhere near the urge.
2. Read 3 lines off the BLUE LIST.
3. Your ethos, once. Your one intention off Practice Intentions, out loud.

THE DOOR - every time you walk into the gym
Your Polaris trigger: be intentional, be relentless, be aggressive.
Check the gauge on the way in. Too hot: 3 DOWN breaths. Flat: UP breaths and move. Ready: go.
First possession is an effort job. Sprint the floor, hit someone on a screen, talk. Something you cannot fail.

FREE THROWS - the same routine every time, practice and games
1. Feet on your spot.
2. Hot: one DOWN breath.
3. Your dribbles. Same number every time.
4. Eyes on one exact spot on the rim. Hold them dead still a beat longer than feels normal, then shoot without moving them. That still last look is the quiet eye, one of the most researched shooting habits there is, and it holds up under pressure.
5. One feel word as you rise, never mechanics. Yours: ___
6. Hold the follow-through. Make or miss, then the reset.

THE RESET - after every mistake, 3 seconds
1. One physical cue. Wipe your hands on your shorts or pull the jersey. Same one every time.
2. One DOWN breath. Recognize it, release it on the exhale, return. The 6 R's in one breath.
3. Eyes up to the next job: the ball, your man's chest. Be where your eyes and feet are.
No replaying it until film. Same reset after a good play, because a good play you are still thinking about is the next mistake.
Groove it for free: after every miss in 50/50 and every wrong call in READS.

GONE COLD - the opposite of everything above
You will know it: passing up open shots, body heavy, hoping the play goes somewhere else. Slow breathing sinks you further here.
1. UP breaths. Sprint to your spot on the next dead ball.
2. Eyes OUT. The rim, his chest, the ball. Cold lives inside your head.
3. Voice. Call every screen, every switch, loud.
4. One effort goal for the next three possessions that skill cannot ruin. Every one you finish is blue.
An open shot is still shot. Hesitating is the symptom, not a fix.

CHECK-IN - off the bench (Polaris)
At the table: your 2/1 breathing, then the door. First job is an effort play.

SUB-OUT (Polaris)
Encourage a teammate. Ask a coach what they see. One thought: my job when I go back in. Then watch your man. No replaying.

JUDGMENT, IN THE MOMENT
Their opinion is not the scoreboard. You play to your standard, not to their reaction.
Nick's example: Curry turns around before the ball lands. Give yourself the acceptance first.

AFTER
Tonight: the best proof of the game goes on the BLUE LIST.
Tomorrow: the red gets one look on film, in one set window. Tag it, write the fix, close it.

LAST PRACTICE OR GAME - yes or no, overwrite each time
Slot full walking in? ___
